procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 01.04.2019 of the High Court of Judicature at Madras in CRLA No. 45 of 2014, which set aside the order of the Appellate Court and restored the order of the Trial Court, convicting the appellants.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court convicted the appellants under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The Appellate Court reversed the Trial Court's findings and acquitted the appellants. The High Court, at the instance of the respondent/complainant, set aside the order of the Appellate Court and restored the order of the Trial Court, convicting the appellants.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, M/s New Win Export & Anr., approached the Supreme Court by filing a Special Leave Petition (SLP) to challenge the High Court's order. The First Party agrees to support the Special Leave Petition filed by the Second Party, in order to enable the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India to pass appropriate order as the Hon’ble supreme Court may deem it fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the present. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The impugned order dated 01.04.2019 as well the Trial Court’s order dated 16.10.2012 are set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether in the instant case, conviction under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 could be quashed by the Supreme Court as the parties had settled the dispute among themselves by entering into a settlement agreement.

facts: The appellants were convicted under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act for a dishonored cheque.
After the High Court upheld the conviction, the appellants and the respondent-complainant entered into a settlement agreement while the case was on appeal before the Supreme Court.
As per the agreement, the appellants paid the full cheque amount of Rs. 5,25,000 to the complainant.
The complainant confirmed the settlement and stated they had no objection to the conviction being set aside, which was verified by the Court through an affidavit.
law: Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, states that all offences under the Act are compoundable.
Section 320(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) provides that an offence can be compounded even after a conviction, but it requires the permission of the court where the appeal is pending.
application: The Supreme Court treated the settlement agreement between the parties as a valid compounding of the offence under Section 147 of the NI Act.
The Court satisfied itself of the genuineness of the settlement by requiring the complainant to file an affidavit confirming the terms and their consent.
Since the appeal was pending before it, the Supreme Court had the authority to permit this post-conviction compounding.

The Court reasoned that once the parties have settled the dispute and the complainant has been compensated, upholding the conviction would serve no purpose, especially given the compensatory nature of the remedy under Section 138.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the settlement, allowed the compounding of the offence, and quashed the appellants' conviction, concluding that it would serve no purpose to maintain it after the parties had resolved their dispute.

arguments.issue_text: Whether in the instant case, conviction under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 could be quashed by the Supreme Court as the parties had settled the dispute among themselves by entering into a settlement agreement.
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued that they had entered into a settlement agreement with the respondent-complainant on 27.01.2024.
As per the agreement, they have paid the full settlement amount of Rs. 5,25,000 to the complainant.
Given that the dispute has been settled between the parties, their conviction should be set aside.
respondent_arguments: The respondent-complainant supported the appellants' case by filing an affidavit.
In the affidavit, the respondent admitted that the appellants had paid the amount to their full satisfaction.
The respondent stated that they had no objection to the conviction of the appellants being set aside.

cases.case_name: Raj Reddy Kallem v. The State of Haryana & Anr.
cases.principle: The Supreme Court can quash a conviction under the Negotiable Instruments Act by invoking its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution, even if the complainant declines to give consent for compounding, provided the accused has sufficiently compensated the complainant.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, can be set aside when the parties have settled the dispute, as the conviction would no longer serve any purpose.
obiter: Dishonour of cheques is a regulatory offence which was made an offence only in view of public interest so that the reliability of cheques is not affected.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Considering the totality of the circumstances, specifically the compromise reached between the parties and the full payment of the settlement amount, the court concluded that the conviction of the appellants would no longer serve any purpose. As the compensatory aspect of the law had been fulfilled, the punitive aspect was rendered unnecessary, requiring the conviction to be set aside.
legal_tests_applied: Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, makes all offences under the NI Act compoundable.

Section 320(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, provides that if compounding is to be done after conviction, it can only be done with the leave of the Court where the appeal against such conviction is pending.
why_respondent_won: The parties had entered into a settlement agreement, and the appellants paid the full settlement amount of Rs. 5,25,000 to the respondent-complainant.
The respondent-complainant filed an affidavit admitting that the amount was paid to their full satisfaction and that they had no objection to the conviction being set aside.
The court determined that since the dispute was settled and the compensatory purpose of the law was achieved, the conviction no longer served any purpose.
policy_considerations: Dishonour of cheques is a regulatory offence, created in the public interest to ensure the reliability of these instruments.
The ‘compensatory aspect’ of the remedy under the Negotiable Instruments Act shall have priority over the ‘punitive aspect’.

Courts should encourage the compounding of offences under the NI Act if parties are willing to do so, especially given the large number of pending cases which are a serious concern for the judicial system.
